title: ESP IDE WebSocket message
description: Each WebSocket text message carries one JSON object. The IDE sets ESP_IDE_WS to the socket URL. A tool may set its own URL instead, such as esp-idf-monitor --ws. A diagnostic comes from any tool. Its type is "warning", "error", or "exception". An event comes from esp-idf-monitor. Its type is "event". The IDE replies with an event name such as "debug_finished". That reply can leave type out. Monitor checks the event name only. If the reply includes type, it must be "event".

diagnostic.description: Structured warning, error, or uncaught exception, sent by the tool. Hints, notes, and progress are not sent. Receivers must ignore keys they do not know: later esp-pylib versions can add optional keys to this schema version.

type.description: warning and error carry the console line as plain text, with Rich markup removed and without the WARNING: or ERROR: prefix. exception is an uncaught crash. SystemExit and KeyboardInterrupt are not reported.

source.description: Name the sending tool was started with. For python -m, this is the package name with underscores changed to hyphens, such as "esptool" or "esp-idf-monitor". For a script or command, this is its file name, such as "idf.py", "espefuse", or "gen_esp32part.py". When idf.py runs another tool, the source is that tool, not idf.py. A tool used as a library inside another program reports that program. null if the name is not known, such as for python -c. Older esp-pylib versions leave this field out.

pid.description: Process ID of the sending tool. It is often not the process the IDE started: launchers such as idf.py.exe, console-script .exe files, and the python.exe of a Windows virtual environment start Python as a child process. Older esp-pylib versions leave this field out.

parent_pids.description: Process IDs of the esp-pylib tools that started the sending tool, outermost first. For example, esptool run by idf.py flash lists the idf.py process. Processes that do not use esp-pylib, such as cmake and ninja, are not listed. Empty if no such tool started it. When a tool fails, the tool that started it usually reports a short error of its own, such as "ninja failed with exit code 1". So an error from process P that arrives after an error or exception from a process with P in parent_pids is usually a consequence of that earlier error. Show it as a summary of the earlier error rather than as a separate problem. Do not drop it: a long-running tool such as esp-idf-monitor can report an unrelated error later. Apply this rule within one run only, for example one task the IDE started. Operating systems reuse process IDs, Windows especially quickly, so a tool in a later run can get the PID of a tool from an earlier run. Older esp-pylib versions leave this field out.

file.description: Python file that logged the message, or where the exception was raised. "<unknown>" if the file is not known. This is usually a file inside the tool, not the user's project.

line.description: Line number in file. The first line is 1. Use 0 if the line is not known.

message.description: Text to show the user. For exception, the exception text (which may be empty).

suggestion.description: Extra help text. It is not printed in the terminal. For a crash, this is the traceback, or null if there is none. For a warning or error, this is null unless the tool added a suggested fix.

event.description: A debug message between a tool and the IDE. Extra fields depend on the event name. esp-idf-monitor sends gdb_stub (port, prog), coredump (file, prog), and flash (port, target, full). It then waits for debug_finished or flash_finished. flash_finished may include success as true or false. Other event names are allowed.

type.description: Always present on events sent through esp-pylib. An IDE reply can leave it out. Legacy clients that do not use esp-pylib can also leave it out, so identify an event by its event field.

event.description: Name of the event. The other side waits for this name.
